mappings.note: Which feelings the rains rouse in people -- reading the response the poet works for. Rejected LO-89: the poem names 'subha' but not this range of feeling.

Asks what the children in the PICTURE are doing -- the one item here that turns on looking at an illustration and putting the experience into words. Rejected LO-89: nothing in the verse answers it. NOTE: the figure is not carried in the extracted text, and the key is hedged ('aisa lagta hai') accordingly.

What 'preetam' and 'meetha' are used for and what they carry -- word choice and its force. Rejected LO-86: the demand is lexical. NOTE: the key hedges twice ('prayog kiya ja sakta hai'), which suggests neither word is actually in this poem.
HOW the poem presents the season's beauty -- the poet's handling. Rejected LO-89: the item asks about presentation, not for facts.
Which relation the poet builds between swans and farmers -- a link the reader must draw out. Rejected LO-89: no line states the relation.
What the poem teaches us about the rainy season -- its usefulness. Rejected LO-86: what we take from it, not his handling.
List the natural elements the poem names and their effect -- a collection gathered by close reading. Rejected LO-88: an inventory, not the poem's use.
The message the poet wishes to give -- the poem's usefulness. Rejected LO-86, kept for items about his method.
How peacock and frog are described -- located descriptions. Rejected LO-86: the poem states both.
What the poet means by 'gulaab ki saurabh' -- the word 'saurabh' and its freshness are the demand. Rejected LO-86: a phrase, not a proposition.

The importance of the rains for the ENVIRONMENT -- the key reasons out the water cycle, recharge and agriculture, none of it in the poem, so the learner responds to a real natural issue. Rejected LO-88: not the poem's usefulness but the season's.
The sense of 'varsha-bahaar sabke man ko lubha rahi hai' and the rains' effect on people and children -- explication of the poet's line. Rejected LO-92: the whole line's claim, not one word.
On what ground the poet calls the season 'anokhi', in your own words -- grasping and restating his claim. Rejected LO-92: 'anokhi' is plain; the ground is the point.
A detailed account of the changes in nature and creatures -- assembled from the poem's catalogue. Rejected LO-85: it stays inside the text.
A detailed account of the season's arrival and effects -- again the poem's own inventory. Rejected LO-88: detail, not the message.

Asks how the poet PERSONIFIES cloud, lightning, rose and swan, and what poetic beauty this creates -- maanaveekaran and kaavya-saundarya together. Cited at goal level because none of the 16 outcomes covers a poetic device: LO-90 is folk song and tale specifically, and LO-92 concerns the learner's own use of words, not a poet's figures.
Justify the title and show how the poem brings out nature's beauty -- a judgement about the whole text's fitness. Rejected LO-86: the title's aptness is about the poem as a whole.
How swans and farmers are depicted -- located descriptions. Rejected LO-86, kept for the item asking what relation he builds between them.
How the forest and its creatures are described -- a collection from the poem. Rejected LO-85: description, not reasoning.
Who moves in a fine line (swans), from the printed extract. Rejected CG-HIN3, kept for the symbolism item.
What the rain-splendour is like ('anokhi'), from the extract. Rejected LO-86: the epithet is quoted.
Who sings (the farmers), from the extract. Rejected LO-91: the item asks who, not about farming language.

What the swans' moving in line SYMBOLISES -- reading a pratik, keyed as beauty and discipline. Cited at goal level because no outcome among the 16 covers poetic symbol; LO-90 is folk song and tale specifically.
How the farmers draw people to them -- by their songs of joy, from the extract. Rejected LO-91: the item asks how, not about their trade's vocabulary.
Where the peacocks dance (in the forest). Rejected LO-83: a fact, not a rendering.
Who sings in this extract (the frogs). Rejected LO-86: stated.
What blooms in the garden (roses). Rejected LO-92: no gloss wanted.
What the poet SHOWS us in the forest -- the key reads it as the peacocks' gladness at the rains, an interpretation. Rejected LO-89, used for the bare 'who dances where' item.
How the frogs' calling strikes the POET -- as if singing a sweet song, which is his figure rather than a fact. Rejected LO-89 for that reason.
What draws every heart (the rain-splendour), from the extract. Rejected LO-86: stated.
What the clouds do, from the extract. Rejected LO-86: stated.
Where the lightning flashes (the sky). Rejected LO-86: stated.
What the sky's spread is like -- the extract's own epithets. Rejected LO-92: 'ghanghor' is glossed in its own item.
What happens in the sky during the rains -- three located facts. Rejected LO-85: reported, not reasoned.
The name of the lesson this extract comes from -- placing the text. Rejected LO-89: bibliographic, not inside the verse.
What cooled the wind (the rain) -- located in the extract. Rejected LO-85: a fact.
What moves the branches (the wind). Rejected LO-86: stated.
The visible effect of the cool wind -- swaying branches and the gardeners' wives singing. Rejected LO-86: both stated.
What the poet means by the compound 'jeev jalchar' -- the key unpacks it into the creatures it covers. Rejected LO-89: a gloss, not a located point.
Which season the lines describe -- a judgement about the extract as a whole. Rejected LO-89: no single line names it.
What is happening during the rain -- two located facts. Rejected LO-86: stated.
Meaning of 'ghanghor' -- dense and dark. Rejected LO-89: lexical.
The sense of the whole line about the rains charming every heart -- explication of the poet's claim. Rejected LO-92: a line, not a word.
What the poet says of the waterfalls -- located in the extract. Rejected LO-86: stated.
The mark of the open rose (it spreads fragrance). Rejected LO-92: 'saurabh' is glossed in its own item.
The mood pervading the gardens -- stated in the extract. Rejected LO-92: 'aamod' is glossed in its own item.
Sense of 'aamod chha raha hai' -- the word 'aamod' is the difficulty. Rejected LO-89: lexical.
Sense of 'gaate hain geet kaise, lete kisaan manhar' -- turns on 'manhar', heart-stealing. Rejected LO-86: the words carry it, not a proposition.

Sense of 'gaate hain geet kaise' -- the force of the exclamatory 'kaise'. Rejected LO-86: a phrase. NOTE: this item and the one before it gloss overlapping stretches of the same line and are near duplicates.
